# Government claim verification checklist

> Generated by `npm run verify:report` from `content/`. Do not edit by hand; record results with the commands below and regenerate.

**Progress:** 0 / 622 claims fully verified · 0 verified, 733 unverified, 0 incorrect, 0 unsupported (733 claim–source checks).

## How to verify

1. Open the source URL. Each section below is one source page with every claim that cites it.
2. For each claim, find the sentence on the page that supports it. Numbers must match (rounding like "about" is fine; a different figure is not).
3. Record the result (or fill in the CSV and run `npm run verify:import-csv -- docs/verification/government.csv --by "Your Name"`):
   - **verified**: the page states it. Paste the supporting sentence as the quote.
   - **unsupported**: the page does not say it. Find a better source or change the claim.
   - **incorrect**: the page (or better evidence) contradicts it. The card/question must be revised in a new revision.
4. A level can only be published when every claim it states or teaches is verified against every source it cites. `npm run validate:content` enforces this.

"Pre-check" notes were written while drafting. They point at what to look at closely. They are not verification.

"Fact-check" results come from an automated check against independent sources found by web search (not the cited page, which couldn't be opened). A **corrected** or **disputed** claim was reworded to match those sources; the old wording is shown. They are not verification either: the cited page still has to be checked.

### ☐ `fact.government.rules_dagen_h`: unverified

> **Claim:** On 3 September 1967, Dagen H, Sweden switched from left- to right-hand traffic: early that morning traffic stopped, then every vehicle moved to the right.

- **Concept:** Rules that coordinate: Sweden's Dagen H (`concept.government.rules_coordination_sweden`)
- **Appears in:**
  - L2 “Why Have Rules?” · `card.government.002.c4` (fact): On 3 September 1967, a whole country switched sides of the road. / Swedes call it Dagen H, for högertrafik, right-hand traffic. Early that morning, traffic stopped, then every vehicle moved over to the right. The change had to happen everywhere at once, because a traffic rule only works when everyone follows the same one. Deciding a rule like that for a whole country is a job for Level 1's steering wheel: government.
  - L5 “Public Services” · `card.government.005.c4` (fact): Free riders are beaten by a rule that everyone chips in. / If people agree through the political process to pay taxes, the law can require everyone to contribute, and the public good gets made. It's Level 2's lesson again: a rule works when everybody follows the same one. How those taxes work is the next level.
  - L10 “Checkpoint: Why Government?” · `card.government.010.c3` (comparison): Chapter 1 in three questions: Why rules? (So everyone plays the same game, from football to traffic; Laws bind a whole community and are enforced) vs Who decides? (Authority: power people accept as legitimate; The social contract asks why we obey) vs Who pays, and who does what? (Compulsory taxes fund public services; National, regional and local layers share the work)
- **Tested by:**
  - L2 `question.government.002.q3`: What do the 1863 football rulebook and Sweden's Dagen H have in common? → **Both got everyone following the same rule**
  - L5 `question.government.005.q3`: Level 2 showed that a rule works when everyone follows the same one. How does that help pay for public goods? → **A law makes everyone pay taxes, so no one free rides**
  - L10 `question.government.010.q3`: Why Government? checkpoint: which list puts these in order, oldest first? → **Hammurabi's code → Leviathan → FA rules → Dagen H**
- **Fact-check (2026-09-25):** corroborated. 99% Invisible and History Facts both date the switch to 3 September 1967, with traffic halted just before 5 a.m. and moved to the right side of the road. Sources: https://99percentinvisible.org/episode/h-day/, https://historyfacts.com/world-history/fact/sweden-switched-driving-left-to-right/

```sh
npm run verify:record -- fact.government.rules_dagen_h source.99pi_h_day --status verified --by "Your Name" --quote "…"
```

### ☐ `fact.government.election_alternative_vote`: unverified

> **Claim:** Under the Alternative Vote, used for Australia's House of Representatives, voters rank candidates; if no one has a majority, the least successful are eliminated and their votes transferred by next preference until someone does.

- **Concept:** Ranked voting (`concept.government.election_ranked_choice`)
- **Appears in:**
  - L63 “Voting Systems” · `card.government.063.c4` (text): Ranked choice / Ranked systems ask for more than one choice. Australia's House of Representatives uses the Alternative Vote: rank the candidates, and if nobody has a majority, the least successful are eliminated and their votes pass to next preferences until someone does. Ireland's Single Transferable Vote uses rankings in districts that elect several members, keeping results fairly proportional.
- **Tested by:**
  - L70 `question.government.070.q3`: Back to Level 63: under the Alternative Vote used for Australia's House of Representatives, what happens if nobody has a majority? → **The last are eliminated and votes transferred**
- **Fact-check (2026-09-25):** corroborated. IDEA handbook: AV used in Australia; least successful candidates eliminated and votes reallocated until one has an absolute majority. AEC: House of Representatives counts transfer votes by preference until a candidate has an absolute majority. Sources: https://www.aec.gov.au/learn/preferential-voting.htm, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Instant-runoff_voting

  - L33 “Changing a Constitution” · `card.government.033.c3` (text): The American hurdle, and a two-century wait / Under Article V, an amendment needs two-thirds of both houses of Congress (or a convention) to propose it and three-fourths of the states to ratify it. In 2017 his university changed his grade to an A.

### ☐ `fact.government.suffrage_15th_amendment`: unverified

> **Claim:** The 15th Amendment, ratified in 1870, says the vote shall not be denied or abridged on account of race, color, or previous condition of servitude.

- **Concept:** Voting amendments in the U.S. Constitution (`concept.government.rights_voting_amendments`)
- **Appears in:**
  - L37 “Who Gets to Vote” · `card.government.037.c3` (timeline): America's line, moved by amendment: 1870: 15th Amendment: no denying the vote on account of race, color or previous servitude; 1964: 24th Amendment: no poll tax as a condition of voting in federal elections; 1971: 26th Amendment: no denying the vote on account of age to citizens 18 or older
  - L39 “Civil Rights” · `card.government.039.c4` (text): A promise kept 95 years late / Remember Level 37's 15th Amendment of 1870? Southern states had long kept Black citizens from voting anyway, with tools like literacy tests. After state troopers attacked peaceful marchers in Selma, Alabama, national attention helped persuade Congress to act. The Voting Rights Act, signed on 6 August 1965, outlawed literacy tests as a condition of voting. It enforced the 15th Amendment, 95 years after its ratification.
- **Tested by:**

  - L39 `question.government.039.q3`: The Voting Rights Act of 1965 was built to enforce which amendment from Level 37? → **The 15th, ratified 95 years earlier**

### ☐ `fact.government.constitution_us_bill_of_rights_1791`: unverified

> **Claim:** The first ten amendments to the U.S. Constitution, ratified in 1791, are known as the Bill of Rights.

- **Concept:** Inside the U.S. Constitution (`concept.government.constitution_us_structure`)
- **Appears in:**
  - L32 “The U.S. Constitution” · `card.government.032.c5` (fact): Its first ten amendments, ratified in 1791, are called the Bill of Rights. / The original articles mostly build the machinery of government. The Bill of Rights added guarantees for people, starting with the First Amendment: "Congress shall make no law respecting an establishment of religion," plus protections for speech, the press, assembly and petition. Several levels in this chapter start right there.
  - L36 “Privacy” · `card.government.036.c3` (text): The missing word in the U.S. Constitution / Search the U.S. Constitution for "privacy" and you won't find it. Courts built the right from parts of Level 32's Bill of Rights, especially the First, Fourth and Fifth Amendments. The Fourth protects people "in their persons, houses, papers, and effects" against unreasonable searches and seizures, and requires warrants based on probable cause. In 1965 the Supreme Court described a "zone of privacy" formed by these guarantees.
- **Tested by:**
  - L36 `question.government.036.q3`: The U.S. Constitution never uses the word "privacy." Where did courts find the right? → **In Bill of Rights amendments such as the Fourth**
- **Fact-check (2026-09-25):** corroborated. The National Archives says the Bill of Rights was ratified on 15 December 1791, when three-fourths of the states approved ten of twelve proposed amendments; Wikipedia's list of amendments gives 15 December 1791 for the first ten. Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_amendments_to_the_United_States_Constitution

### ☐ `fact.government.statehood_montevideo_criteria`: unverified

> **Claim:** The Montevideo Convention, signed on 26 December 1933, says a state should have a permanent population, a defined territory, a government and the capacity to enter into relations with other states.

- **Appears in:**
  - L81 “Sovereignty” · `card.government.081.c4` (text): A four-point checklist / How do you recognize a state? The Montevideo Convention, signed in 1933, lists four qualifications: a permanent population, a defined territory, a government, and the capacity to enter into relations with other states. Level 9's state already had territory and laws; the fourth test looks outward. And Article 3 adds a twist: a state's existence doesn't depend on other states recognizing it.
  - L82 “Diplomacy” · `card.government.082.c2` (text): What an embassy is for / An embassy is one country's permanent office inside another. The Vienna Convention lists its jobs: represent its country, protect its interests and citizens, negotiate with the host government, report home on what's happening, and promote friendly relations. None of it is forced: diplomatic relations are set up by mutual consent. Level 81's fourth test for a state was the capacity to enter into relations with other states. Embassies are that capacity at work.
- **Tested by:**

  - L82 `question.government.082.q3`: Which of Level 81's four tests for statehood do embassies put into practice? → **The capacity to enter into relations with other states**
  - L88 `question.government.088.q3`: UNHCR says refugee status is declaratory. Which Level 81 rule about states works the same way? → **A state's existence doesn't depend on recognition**
- **Fact-check (2026-09-25):** corroborated. The convention text on the Avalon Project gives the four qualifications in Article 1; Britannica gives the 26 December 1933 signing date and the same criteria. Sources: https://avalon.law.yale.edu/20th_century/intam03.asp, https://www.britannica.com/event/Montevideo-Convention, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Montevideo_Convention

Restrictions must be set by law and be necessary, for example to respect the rights or reputations of others, or to protect national security, public order, or public health or morals. Notice the key word in Article 21: peaceful. And remember Level 4: a law is a rule the community recognizes as binding. Here, law is what marks where the megaphone stops.
  - L31 “What a Constitution Is” · `card.government.031.c2` (text): The rules for making rules / Level 4 defined a law as a rule the whole community is bound by. A constitution sits one floor up. Britannica calls it the body of doctrines and practices that form the fundamental organizing principle of a state. International IDEA puts it more simply: a constitution is the supreme law of a country, and ordinary laws are made inside the framework it sets. It's the rulebook for the people who write the rulebooks.

Embassies are that capacity at work.

### ☐ `fact.government.social_contract_definition`: unverified

> **Claim:** A social contract is an actual or hypothetical agreement between the ruled, or between rulers and ruled, setting out the rights and duties of each.

- **Concept:** The social contract and Hobbes (`concept.government.social_contract_hobbes`)
- **Appears in:**
  - L7 “The Social Contract” · `card.government.007.c1` (text): You never signed a contract with your government. Some say you're in one anyway. / A social contract is an agreement, real or imagined, between the people, or between the people and their rulers, setting out the rights and duties of each. Three thinkers used the idea to tackle one question: why obey a government at all? Each gave a different answer.
  - L10 “Checkpoint: Why Government?” · `card.government.010.c3` (comparison): Chapter 1 in three questions: Why rules? (So everyone plays the same game, from football to traffic; Laws bind a whole community and are enforced) vs Who decides? (Authority: power people accept as legitimate; The social contract asks why we obey) vs Who pays, and who does what? (Compulsory taxes fund public services; National, regional and local layers share the work)
  - L10 “Checkpoint: Why Government?” · `card.government.010.c4` (text): Back at the helm / Level 1 began with a ship. Now you can name its parts. The rules of the voyage are laws. Whoever holds the wheel needs authority, and the social contract asks why the crew goes along. The cargo everyone shares is public services. Taxes pay for the fuel. And the crew works on several decks at once, from the national government to the village council.
  - L48 “Unjust Laws” · `card.government.048.c4` (text): Socrates: stay and obey / In Plato's Crito, Socrates makes the opposite choice. Awaiting execution, he refuses a chance to escape, though he thinks his sentence unjust. By living in Athens all his life, he argues, he had implicitly agreed to obey its laws. Sound like Level 7's social contract? It's the same idea, told as a prison conversation.
  - L92 “Rights and Responsibilities” · `card.government.092.c2` (text): Rights come with responsibilities / Canada's official citizenship guide puts it in one line: in Canada, rights come with responsibilities. It's an old idea. Level 7's social contract set out the rights and duties of each side, and Level 91's citizenship trades allegiance for protection. You don't just hold rights. You help keep up the system that protects them.
- **Tested by:**
  - L48 `question.government.048.q3`: In the Crito, Socrates says living in Athens meant he had implicitly agreed to its laws. Which Level 7 idea does that echo? → **The social contract**
  - L100 `question.government.100.q5`: Canada's citizenship guide says rights come with responsibilities. Which Level 7 idea says much the same? → **The social contract, setting out rights and duties of each side**

### ☐ `fact.government.presumption_reasonable_doubt`: unverified

> **Claim:** In criminal cases the prosecution must prove guilt beyond reasonable doubt; if a reasonable doubt remains, the accused is acquitted.

In criminal cases, the prosecution has to prove guilt beyond reasonable doubt; if a reasonable doubt remains, the accused goes free. The system is tilted on purpose. In the 1760s William Blackstone put it in one line: it is better that ten guilty persons escape than that one innocent suffer.
  - L56 “Criminal and Civil Law” · `card.government.056.c4` (text): Two different bars / Here's the key. Criminal guilt must be proved beyond reasonable doubt. A civil claim needs only to be more likely than not: the balance of probabilities, anything over 50%. So a jury can have a reasonable doubt that Simpson committed murder, while another decides it's more likely than not he was responsible. Same facts, two bars, two answers.
  - L60 “Checkpoint: Courts and Justice” · `card.government.060.c2` (text): The scales: weighing the case / Justice comes from a Roman virtue, and her scales came to stand for impartiality. That's Level 51's courts, weighing facts against the law. It's Level 53's jurors, weighing the evidence. And it's Level 54's rule for how the scales start: tipped toward the accused, until the prosecution proves guilt beyond reasonable doubt.

- **URL:** https://www.congress.gov/help/learn-about-the-legislative-process/how-our-laws-are-made
- **License:** reference_only · **Accessed:** 2026-09-25 · **Source record checked (URL/licence):** no

### ☐ `fact.government.lawmaking_us_identical_text`: unverified

> **Claim:** In the United States, a bill must be passed by both the House and the Senate in identical form before it goes to the President to be signed into law.

- **Concept:** The stages of a bill (`concept.government.lawmaking_bill_stages`)
- **Appears in:**
  - L41 “How a Bill Becomes Law” · `card.government.041.c4` (text): Every word agreed / Both Houses must agree the exact wording. If the Lords change something the Commons won't accept, the bill bounces back and forth between them, a process nicknamed ping-pong, until they settle. The US works the same way: the House and the Senate must pass a bill in identical form before it goes to the President to be signed. A law is born only when both chambers agree on every word.
- **Tested by:**
  - L41 `question.government.041.q2`: Why can a bill bounce back and forth between the Commons and the Lords before Royal Assent? → **Both Houses must agree its exact wording**
  - L45 `question.government.045.q3`: A US bill has passed the House and the Senate in identical form. What can still stop it becoming law? → **A presidential veto that Congress fails to override**
  - L50 `question.government.050.q3`: Making Laws milestone: which order is right for a US bill that the President vetoes? → **Both chambers pass it → President vetoes → two-thirds of each override**
- **Fact-check (2026-09-25):** corroborated. CRS report 98-696 on Congress.gov: enactment requires both chambers to agree to the same bill in the same form before presenting it to the President; Senate.gov describes the same. Sources: https://www.congress.gov/crs-product/98-696, https://www.senate.gov/legislative/common/briefing/leg_laws_acts.htm

```sh
npm run verify:record -- fact.government.lawmaking_us_identical_text source.congress_how_our_laws_are_made --status verified --by "Your Name" --quote "…"
```

## Veto Power (Article I, Section 7, Clause 2) (Constitution Annotated, Congress.gov)

- **Source:** `source.constitution_annotated_veto`
- **URL:** https://constitution.congress.gov/browse/essay/artI-S7-C2-2/ALDE_00013645/
- **License:** reference_only · **Accessed:** 2026-09-25 · **Source record checked (URL/licence):** no

### ☐ `fact.government.lawmaking_veto_pocket`: unverified

> **Claim:** If Congress adjourns so that the President cannot return a bill within the 10 days, the bill is pocket vetoed, and Congress cannot override a pocket veto.

- **Concept:** The US veto and override (`concept.government.lawmaking_veto_us_process`)
- **Appears in:**
  - L45 “The Veto” · `card.government.045.c2` (text): Sign it or send it back / A veto is an executive's power to reject a bill, preventing it from becoming law. In the US, the President has 10 days (Sundays excepted) to sign a bill or return it to Congress with objections. Congress can override a veto, but only by a two-thirds vote in each chamber. And if Congress adjourns so the President can't return the bill, it's a pocket veto, which can't be overridden at all.
- **Tested by:**
  - L45 `question.government.045.q3`: A US bill has passed the House and the Senate in identical form. What can still stop it becoming law? → **A presidential veto that Congress fails to override**
  - L50 `question.government.050.q3`: Making Laws milestone: which order is right for a US bill that the President vetoes? → **Both chambers pass it → President vetoes → two-thirds of each override**
  - L50 `question.government.050.q7`: Making Laws milestone: ending a Senate filibuster and overriding a US veto both require what? → **A supermajority, more than a simple majority**
- **Fact-check (2026-09-25):** corroborated. CRS "Regular Vetoes and Pocket Vetoes": a pocket veto occurs when adjournment prevents return within 10 days and cannot be overridden; Britannica says the pocket veto is absolute. Sources: https://www.congress.gov/crs-product/RS22188, https://www.britannica.com/topic/veto

```sh
npm run verify:record -- fact.government.lawmaking_veto_pocket source.constitution_annotated_veto --status verified --by "Your Name" --quote "…"
```

## How a C-grade college term paper led to a constitutional amendment (National Constitution Center)

- **Source:** `source.constitutioncenter_27th_watson`
- **URL:** https://constitutioncenter.org/blog/how-a-c-grade-college-term-paper-led-to-a-constitutional-amendment
- **License:** reference_only · **Accessed:** 2026-09-25 · **Source record checked (URL/licence):** no

### ☐ `fact.government.amendment_27th_dates`: unverified

> **Claim:** The 27th Amendment, which delays changes to congressional pay until after the next House election, was proposed on 25 September 1789 and ratified on 7 May 1992.

- **Concept:** The 27th Amendment and Gregory Watson (`concept.government.amendment_27th_watson`)
- **Appears in:**
  - L33 “Changing a Constitution” · `card.government.033.c1` (text): In 1982 a student got a C on a paper. Then he helped amend the Constitution. / Gregory Watson, a sophomore at the University of Texas at Austin, wrote about a congressional pay amendment proposed back in 1789. Congress had never set a deadline for ratifying it, he argued, so it was still pending. His professor wasn't convinced and gave him a C. So Watson started writing to state lawmakers.
  - L33 “Changing a Constitution” · `card.government.033.c3` (text): The American hurdle, and a two-century wait / Under Article V, an amendment needs two-thirds of both houses of Congress (or a convention) to propose it and three-fourths of the states to ratify it. That bar has been cleared just 27 times. Watson's letters helped: the pay amendment, proposed on 25 September 1789, was ratified on 7 May 1992 as the 27th Amendment. In 2017 his university changed his grade to an A.
- **Tested by:**
  - L33 `question.government.033.q1`: What finally happened to the congressional pay amendment that Gregory Watson championed? → **It was ratified in 1992 as the 27th Amendment**
- **Fact-check (2026-09-25):** corroborated. The National Constitution Center's amendment page gives the same text and dates. Sources: https://constitutioncenter.org/the-constitution/amendments/amendment-xxvii
- **Weak evidence:** one-page (revisit first)

In England and Wales that's the Crown Prosecution Service, independent of the police, which decides which police-investigated cases go to court and then prosecutes them.   - L56 “Criminal and Civil Law” · `card.government.056.c2` (text): Criminal: the state brings the case / A criminal case is about an alleged crime. It comes to court when the state decides to prosecute; in England and Wales that decision is usually the Crown Prosecution Service's. The European Court of Auditors agreed in 2018 that PPPs can speed delivery and keep up maintenance. ### ☐ `fact.government.monarchy_word_rule_of_one`: unverified

> **Claim:** The word monarchy comes from the Greek monarkhia, literally 'ruling of one', from monos (alone) and arkhein (to rule).

- **Concept:** Monarchy: rule of one (`concept.government.monarchy_definition`)
- **Appears in:**
  - L11 “Monarchy” · `card.government.011.c2` (text): Rule of one / The name gives it away. Monarchy comes from the Greek monarkhia, literally "ruling of one". Britannica defines it as a system based on the undivided rule of a single person. That person, the monarch, is head of state and usually gets the job by heredity. You don't apply for a throne. You're born next in line for it.
- **Tested by:**
  - L11 `question.government.011.q1`: Monarchy: the Greek word monarkhia literally means what? → **Ruling of one**
  - L11 `question.government.011.q2`: Why is Malaysia's paramount ruler unusual among monarchs? → **He is elected for five years instead of inheriting the throne**
  - L14 `question.government.014.q3`: Rule by the few: judging by their Greek roots, what separates oligarchy from Level 11's monarchy? → **Monarchy is rule by one; oligarchy is rule by a few**
- **Fact-check (2026-09-25):** corroborated. Etymonline gives Greek monarkhia, 'ruling of one', from monos + arkhein; Britannica defines monarchy as the rule of a single person. Sources: https://www.etymonline.com/word/monarchy, https://www.britannica.com/topic/monarchy

### ☐ `fact.government.parliament_word_parler`: unverified

> **Claim:** The word parliament comes from Old French parlement, 'a speaking, talk', from parler, 'to speak'.

- **Concept:** Parliaments: old roots, one or two chambers (`concept.government.parliament_althing_chambers`)
- **Appears in:**
  - L23 “Parliaments” · `card.government.023.c2` (text): A place for talking / Parliament comes from the Old French parlement, "a speaking, talk", from parler, "to speak". That's the core of it: a room (or, in Iceland's case, a site) where a country's representatives argue things out in the open before anything is decided. Kings could simply give orders; a parliament has to talk things through first.
  - L30 “Checkpoint: Democracy” · `card.government.030.c4` (text): From a Greek word to a working machine / The chapter began with demokratia, rule by the people, and Lincoln's government of, by and for the people. Everything since is machinery for making that phrase true: parliaments that talk before they decide, prime ministers who can lose parliament's confidence, presidents elected for fixed terms, parties that organize voters and opposition, and reporters in the gallery.
- **Tested by:**

- **Fact-check (2026-09-25):** corroborated. Etymonline: from Old French parlement 'a speaking, talk', from parler. Britannica's parliament article: the word originally meant 'a talk'. Sources: https://www.etymonline.com/word/parliament, https://www.britannica.com/topic/parliament

## Aims and values (European Union)

- **Source:** `source.eu_aims_values`
- **URL:** https://european-union.europa.eu/principles-countries-history/principles-and-values/aims-and-values_en
- **License:** reference_only · **Accessed:** 2026-09-25 · **Source record checked (URL/licence):** no

### ☐ `fact.government.eu_founded_on_treaties`: unverified

> **Claim:** Everything the EU does is founded on treaties voluntarily and democratically agreed by its member countries.

- **Concept:** How the EU makes laws (`concept.government.eu_lawmaking`)
- **Appears in:**
  - L85 “The European Union” · `card.government.085.c3` (text): Laws made in a triangle / Everything the EU does rests on treaties its member countries agreed to voluntarily and democratically. Lawmaking runs through a triangle. The European Commission proposes a law. Two bodies adopt it: the European Parliament, directly elected by EU citizens, and the Council of the EU, where ministers from each member government sit. The member countries then put it into practice, and the Commission checks that they do.
  - L85 “The European Union” · `card.government.085.c4` (text): Sharing the final say / Remember Level 81: sovereignty means having the final say. EU members agreed, by treaty, to make some of their laws together, through a Parliament and a Council they all share, instead of each deciding alone. The final say hasn't vanished: in treaties they chose to sign, the members agreed to share some of it.
- **Tested by:**
  - L85 `question.government.085.q2`: In the EU's lawmaking triangle, what is the European Commission's role? → **It proposes new EU laws**
  - L85 `question.government.085.q3`: How does EU membership fit Level 81's idea of sovereignty as having the final say? → **Members agreed by treaty to decide some laws together**
- **Fact-check (2026-09-25):** corroborated. The EU's aims and values page states this under the rule of law; the European Commission's law page says every EU action is founded on treaties approved democratically by its members. Sources: https://european-union.europa.eu/principles-countries-history/principles-and-values/aims-and-values_en, https://commission.europa.eu/about/role/law_en

```sh
npm run verify:record -- fact.government.eu_founded_on_treaties source.eu_aims_values --status verified --by "Your Name" --quote "…"
```

> **Claim:** Only states may be parties in cases before the ICJ; its jurisdiction rests on the consent of the states involved, and it also gives advisory opinions when UN bodies ask.

And a state can't simply be dragged in: the Court's jurisdiction rests on the consent of the states involved. (Embassies represent, negotiate and report; Their premises can't be entered without consent) vs How do they make promises? ### ☐ `fact.government.amendment_harder_than_laws`: unverified

> **Claim:** Most constitutions make amending harder than passing ordinary laws, using a legislative supermajority, a referendum, a double decision (sometimes with an intervening election) or approval by states or regions.

- **Concept:** How constitutions are amended (`concept.government.amendment_entrenchment`)
- **Appears in:**
  - L33 “Changing a Constitution” · `card.government.033.c2` (text): Harder than a law, on purpose / Constitutions must be able to change, but most make amending harder than passing an ordinary law. The usual hurdles: a supermajority in the legislature, a referendum, a double decision (sometimes with an election in between), or approval by the states or regions. Why bother? Too rigid, and needed reforms get stuck. Too flexible, and whoever holds power can wear away the rights and institutions the constitution protects.
- **Tested by:**
  - L33 `question.government.033.q2`: Why do most constitutions make amending harder than passing an ordinary law? → **So those in power can't easily wear away rights and institutions**
- **Fact-check (2026-09-25):** corroborated. Britannica's US example shows these hurdles: proposal by two-thirds of both houses and approval by three-fourths of the states. Sources: https://www.britannica.com/topic/constitution-politics-and-law, https://constitutionnet.org/vl/item/constitutional-amendment-procedures

### ☐ `fact.government.amendment_ireland_procedure`: unverified

> **Claim:** In Ireland, an amendment is passed by parliament in the same way as an ordinary law and then needs approval by a majority of votes cast in a referendum.

- **Concept:** How constitutions are amended (`concept.government.amendment_entrenchment`)
- **Appears in:**
  - L33 “Changing a Constitution” · `card.government.033.c4` (text): Some countries ask everyone / Other countries set the bar differently. Some require a referendum for every amendment, however small: Australia, Denmark, Ireland and Japan among them. ### ☐ `fact.government.election_popper_dismissal`: unverified

> **Claim:** Karl Popper, in The Open Society and Its Enemies (1945), held that in a democracy the ruled can dismiss their rulers without bloodshed, for example through general elections.

- **Appears in:**
  - L61 “Why Elections?” · `card.government.061.c1` (text): Every few years, whole countries can fire their government. Nobody gets hurt. / Swapping the people in charge of a country, peacefully and on a schedule, is an odd thing when you stop to think about it. So what exactly are elections for? An economist, a philosopher and the United Nations each gave an answer.
  - L61 “Why Elections?” · `card.government.061.c3` (text): Popper: the power to fire / The philosopher Karl Popper, author of The Open Society and Its Enemies (1945), shifted the question. "The people do not rule anywhere," he wrote; governments rule. What matters is that the ruled can dismiss their rulers without bloodshed, for example through general elections. For Popper, the test of a democracy isn't who wins. It's whether today's winners can be voted out tomorrow.
  - L70 “Checkpoint: Elections” · `card.government.070.c3` (text): From a ballot to power / Follow one vote through this chapter. It's cast in secret, turned into seats by a voting system and a district map, fought over in a campaign and counted in the open. What comes out is Level 3's authority: power people accept as legitimate. And Popper's point makes it complete: the ruled can dismiss their rulers without bloodshed, so next time the same vote can take that power away.

- **Fact-check (2026-09-25):** corroborated. IEP: The Open Society (1945); democracy offers a nonviolent, institutionalized way to get rid of bad rulers by voting them out. Popper's Open Society ch. 19 (quoted widely): rulers can be dismissed by the ruled without bloodshed. Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Open_Society_and_Its_Enemies, https://mises.org/journal-libertarian-studies/visualizing-karl-poppers-open-society-and-its-enemies

### ☐ `fact.government.naturalization_canada_days`: unverified

> **Claim:** Applicants for Canadian citizenship must have been physically in Canada for at least 1,095 days (3 years) during the 5 years before they apply.

- **Concept:** Naturalization (`concept.government.citizenship_naturalization`)
- **Appears in:**
  - L91 “Citizenship” · `card.government.091.c4` (fact): Adults can join too. Canada asks for 1,095 days first. / Becoming a citizen by applying is called naturalization. > **Claim:** Canada's Constitution Act, 1867 gives provinces power over municipal institutions; courts have called municipalities "creatures" of the provincial legislature, with only the powers provincial law confers.

### ☐ `fact.government.audit_lima_declaration`: unverified

> **Claim:** The Lima Declaration, adopted in 1977 by the world's supreme audit institutions, is known as the Magna Carta of government auditing; its chief aim is to call for independent government auditing.

- **Concept:** Auditing public money (`concept.government.audit_supreme_institutions`)
- **Appears in:**
  - L80 “Checkpoint: Money and Government” · `card.government.080.c2` (text): Auditors who answer to no minister / Countries' top auditors are called supreme audit institutions. In 1977 they adopted the Lima Declaration, known as the Magna Carta of government auditing, and its chief aim is independent auditing. Level 76's European Court of Auditors shows the job: it asked not only 'was the money spent?' but 'did it deliver?', and found PPPs running up to 52 months late.
  - L80 “Checkpoint: Money and Government” · `card.government.080.c4` (comparison): Chapter 8 on one receipt: Raise and borrow (Compulsory taxes pay for most of it; Deficits are borrowed, and pile up as debt) vs Plan and spend (Prepare, approve, carry out, audit; Social protection is the biggest slice) vs Check (Independent auditors check spending; Bodies like Hong Kong's ICAC fight corruption)
- **Tested by:**
  - L80 `question.government.080.q1`: What is the chief aim of the 1977 Lima Declaration on government auditing? → **Independent government auditing**
  - L80 `question.government.080.q2`: The European Court of Auditors asked whether PPP money delivered results, not just whether it was spent. What does that show about auditing? → **Auditors check results as well as receipts**
- **Fact-check (2026-09-25):** corroborated. Peru's Comptroller General site for the Declaration's 40th anniversary and the IDI describe the 1977 Lima Declaration as the Magna Carta of government auditing, centred on independence. ### ☐ `fact.government.lawmaking_traditions_juriglobe_five`: unverified

> **Claim:** The University of Ottawa's JuriGlobe project sorts the world's legal systems into five categories: civil law, common law, customary law, Muslim law and mixed systems.

- **Concept:** Legal traditions around the world (`concept.government.lawmaking_legal_traditions_mixed_world`)
- **Appears in:**
  - L49 “Laws Around the World” · `card.government.049.c4` (text): Custom, religion and mixtures / JuriGlobe, a University of Ottawa project, sorts the world's legal systems into five categories: civil law, common law, customary law, Muslim law and mixed systems. ### ☐ `fact.government.debt_accumulates_bonds`: unverified

> **Claim:** Governments borrow to cover deficits, so recurring deficits accumulate as public debt; 79.3% of public debt in OECD countries takes the form of debt securities such as government bonds.

- **Concept:** Deficits, surpluses and how debt builds up (`concept.government.debt_deficit_balance`)
- **Appears in:**
  - L78 “Deficits and Debt” · `card.government.078.c2` (text): The yearly gap / Level 71's budget has two sides. When spending beats revenue, the gap is a deficit; the reverse is a surplus. To cover a deficit, a government borrows, mostly by selling bonds: 79.3% of OECD public debt takes that form. Run deficits year after year and they pile up as debt.
  - L80 “Checkpoint: Money and Government” · `card.government.080.c3` (text): Follow one euro / Try it with a single euro of tax. It arrives on the collecting side of Level 71's budget. The biggest share of spending goes on social protection, so it may well end up in someone's pension. If the government spent more than it collected, some of what it spent was borrowed. And after the year ends, an auditor checks that the money went where the budget said.
  - L80 “Checkpoint: Money and Government” · `card.government.080.c4` (comparison): Chapter 8 on one receipt: Raise and borrow (Compulsory taxes pay for most of it; Deficits are borrowed, and pile up as debt) vs Plan and spend (Prepare, approve, carry out, audit; Social protection is the biggest slice) vs Check (Independent auditors check spending; Bodies like Hong Kong's ICAC fight corruption)
- **Tested by:**
  - L78 `question.government.078.q1`: In a government's yearly accounts, when is the fiscal balance a deficit? → **When spending is greater than revenue**
  - L78 `question.government.078.q3`: Level 71 showed a budget has a collecting side and a spending side. How does government debt grow from that? → **Spending above collections is borrowed, and the borrowing piles up**
- **Fact-check (2026-09-25):** corroborated. The US Treasury's Fiscal Data guide explains that deficits are financed by borrowing, largely by issuing Treasury securities, which adds to the debt. Sources: https://fiscaldata.treasury.gov/americas-finance-guide/national-deficit/
- **Weak evidence:** one-page (revisit first)

### ☐ `fact.government.health_compulsory_insurance`: unverified

> **Claim:** In France, Germany, Luxembourg and Japan, more than three-quarters of health spending goes through compulsory health insurance, financed mainly by contributions from employers and employees.

- **Concept:** Ways countries pay for healthcare (`concept.government.health_financing_models`)
- **Appears in:**
  - L74 “Healthcare Systems” · `card.government.074.c2` (comparison): Three ways to pay the doctor: Government schemes (Care based on where you live, funded mostly by taxes; 80%+ of spending in Sweden, Norway, Denmark, UK) vs Compulsory insurance (Funded by contributions from employers and employees; Over three-quarters in France, Germany, Japan) vs Out of pocket (Patients pay directly; Over a third of spending in Mexico, Chile, Latvia, Greece)
  - L74 “Healthcare Systems” · `card.government.074.c3` (text): Pipes, not boxes / Most countries mix the pipes rather than pick one. In a government scheme, you're covered because you live there, and the bill goes to the taxpayer. In compulsory insurance, you're covered because contributions are paid for you, usually by you and your employer together. Neither is free; they differ in who writes the cheque and how. Out-of-pocket payments are the leftover, and in some countries it's a big leftover.
- **Tested by:**
  - L74 `question.government.074.q1`: In France, Germany and Japan, how is most health spending financed? → **Compulsory insurance funded by employer and employee contributions**

- **Fact-check (2026-09-25):** corroborated. World Health Systems Facts, drawing on 2023 data, shows compulsory health insurance financing about 78% of German health spending; OECD country notes show mandatory schemes covering 84-86% of spending in France, Germany and Japan. Sources: https://healthsystemsfacts.org/national-health-systems/bismarck-model/germany/germany-health-system-expenditures/, https://www.oecd.org/en/publications/health-at-a-glance-2025_15a55280-en/germany_99d672fb-en.html

### ☐ `fact.government.infra_ppp_definition`: unverified

> **Claim:** The OECD defines public-private partnerships as long-term agreements in which a private partner delivers and funds public services using a capital asset, sharing the risks.

In the OECD's definition, it's a long-term deal in which a private company funds and delivers a public service, like a road, and shares the risks. The European Court of Auditors agreed in 2018 that PPPs can speed delivery and keep up maintenance. ### ☐ `fact.government.free_rider_definition`: unverified

> **Claim:** Free riding means letting others pay for a public good while you enjoy it without paying.

- **Concept:** Public goods and free riders (`concept.government.public_goods_free_riders`)
- **Appears in:**
  - L5 “Public Services” · `card.government.005.c3` (text): Why not just buy them? / Some things are hard to sell one customer at a time. Economists call them public goods: it's hard to stop anyone using them, and one person's use doesn't leave less for others. National defense is the classic case. It protects you whether you paid or not. So why pay? Letting others pay while you enjoy the benefit is called free riding.
  - L89 “Problems Without Borders” · `card.government.089.c3` (text): Free riders, planet-sized / Remember Level 5's free riders, who enjoy a public good while letting others pay? Political scientists describe climate change the same way: a collective action problem, where a country can benefit from free riding on other countries' efforts. At home, a law can require everyone to chip in. Between sovereign countries there's no world government to do that (Level 84), so they make treaties instead.
- **Tested by:**

  - L89 `question.government.089.q3`: Level 5 defined free riding. How does it show up in climate change between countries? → **A country can benefit from others' cuts without its own**
  - L100 `question.government.100.q3`: Level 5's free riders and Level 94's volunteers are near opposites. Why? → **Free riders take without paying; volunteers give without being required**
- **Fact-check (2026-09-25):** corroborated. OpenStax: people have an incentive to let others pay for the public good and then free ride; EconLib describes the same free-rider problem. ### ☐ `fact.government.authority_accepted_power`: unverified

> **Claim:** Authority is accepted power: power that people agree to follow because they see it as legitimate.

- **Concept:** Power versus authority (`concept.government.power_vs_authority`)
- **Appears in:**
  - L3 “Power and Authority” · `card.government.003.c3` (text): Authority: power people accept / Authority is accepted power: power that people agree to follow because they see it as legitimate. For Weber, being obeyed wasn't enough. The order had to be accepted as valid. You wave back at the traffic officer; you don't wave back at the robber. Same stop, very different reason.
  - L4 “What a Law Is” · `card.government.004.c2` (text): Rules versus laws / Your household might ban shoes indoors. That's a rule, but not a law. Britannica describes law as the rules of conduct that a community recognizes as binding, enforced through a controlling authority. Two things make the difference: the whole community is bound by it, and an authority (Level 3's accepted power) stands ready to enforce it.
  - L7 “The Social Contract” · `card.government.007.c3` (text): Locke: government works for you / John Locke saw it differently. Even without government, he argued, people have natural rights to life, liberty and property. Government gets its legitimacy from the consent of the governed, and if rulers violate those rights, people may resist them. Remember Level 3's authority, power people accept? Locke made that acceptance the whole foundation.
  - L9 “Nations and States” · `card.government.009.c3` (text): Weber's test for a state / Remember Max Weber from Level 3? In 1919 he defined the state as a human community that successfully claims the monopoly of the legitimate use of physical force within a territory. Only the state gets to use force, through police and courts, and people accept that it's allowed to. It's Level 3's authority, stretched across a whole country.
  - L10 “Checkpoint: Why Government?” · `card.government.010.c3` (comparison): Chapter 1 in three questions: Why rules? (So everyone plays the same game, from football to traffic; Laws bind a whole community and are enforced) vs Who decides? (Authority: power people accept as legitimate; The social contract asks why we obey) vs Who pays, and who does what? (Compulsory taxes fund public services; National, regional and local layers share the work)
  - L10 “Checkpoint: Why Government?” · `card.government.010.c4` (text): Back at the helm / Level 1 began with a ship. Now you can name its parts. The rules of the voyage are laws. Whoever holds the wheel needs authority, and the social contract asks why the crew goes along. The cargo everyone shares is public services. Taxes pay for the fuel. And the crew works on several decks at once, from the national government to the village council.
  - L13 “Dictatorship” · `card.government.013.c3` (text): How dictators hold on / Modern dictators typically take power by force or fraud, Britannica notes, then keep it through intimidation, terror and the suppression of basic civil liberties. They also use mass propaganda to keep public support. Put that in Level 3's terms. Fear gives them power; propaganda is the effort to make it look like authority, power that people accept.
  - L37 “Who Gets to Vote” · `card.government.037.c4` (text): A world standard: universal and equal / Level 34's Declaration set a benchmark in 1948. Article 21 says the will of the people shall be the basis of the authority of government, expressed in periodic and genuine elections by universal and equal suffrage, held by secret vote. Recall Level 3: authority is power people accept as legitimate. Article 21 names elections as the way that acceptance is expressed.
  - L61 “Why Elections?” · `card.government.061.c4` (text): The UN: where authority comes from / In 1948 the Universal Declaration of Human Rights put a third answer in writing. Article 21 says the will of the people shall be the basis of the authority of government, expressed in periodic and genuine elections. Remember Level 3? Authority is power people accept as legitimate. Elections measure that acceptance again and again instead of assuming it. Locke's consent of the governed, on a timetable.
  - L70 “Checkpoint: Elections” · `card.government.070.c3` (text): From a ballot to power / Follow one vote through this chapter. It's cast in secret, turned into seats by a voting system and a district map, fought over in a campaign and counted in the open. What comes out is Level 3's authority: power people accept as legitimate. And Popper's point makes it complete: the ruled can dismiss their rulers without bloodshed, so next time the same vote can take that power away.
  - L77 “Corruption” · `card.government.077.c2` (text): Borrowed power, misused / Transparency International defines corruption as the abuse of entrusted power for private gain. Every word matters. Entrusted: the power was lent to an official by the public. Abuse: it was used for something it wasn't lent for. Private gain: the official pockets the benefit. Remember Level 3? Authority is power people accept. Corruption quietly turns it into a price list.
- **Tested by:**
  - L3 `question.government.003.q1`: In Weber's terms, what turns power into authority? → **People accepting it as legitimate**
  - L3 `question.government.003.q3`: Level 1's Sumer needed a central authority to share its water. In Weber's terms, what did that authority need beyond power? → **People accepting its orders as valid**
  - L4 `question.government.004.q3`: Level 3 defined authority as accepted power. What role does it play in making a law? → **It stands behind the rule and enforces it**
  - L9 `question.government.009.q3`: Weber said a state claims the monopoly of the legitimate use of force. Which Level 3 idea does "legitimate" point to? → **Authority: power that people accept**
  - L37 `question.government.037.q3`: Level 3 called authority accepted power. According to Article 21 of the Declaration, what should be the basis of a government's authority? → **The will of the people, expressed in genuine elections**
  - L46 `question.government.046.q3`: Level 3 called authority power that people accept as legitimate. What gives a US agency its authority to issue regulations? → **A law enacted by Congress**
  - L61 `question.government.061.q3`: Level 3 said authority is power people accept as legitimate. What does UDHR Article 21 make the basis of government's authority? → **The will of the people, shown in elections**
  - L68 `question.government.068.q3`: Level 3 said authority is power people accept as legitimate. How does counting in front of every candidate's agents help the winner? → **Every side can watch, so the result is easier to accept**
  - L77 `question.government.077.q3`: Level 3 said authority is power people accept as legitimate. In those terms, what does a corrupt official do? → **Uses power the public entrusted to them for private gain**
  - L100 `question.government.100.q2`: A robber and a traffic officer can both make you stop. What does only the officer have, in Weber's terms? → **Authority: power people accept as legitimate**
- **Fact-check (2026-09-25):** corroborated. OpenStax: authority is 'accepted power, that is, power that people agree to follow'.   - L3 “Power and Authority” · `card.government.003.c4` (comparison): Weber's three roots of authority: Traditional (Rests on long-standing custom; Example: a monarch who inherits the throne) vs Charismatic (Rests on a leader's exceptional personal qualities; Examples: Napoleon, Martin Luther King Jr.) vs Legal-rational (Rests on laws and written rules; Belongs to the office, not the person)
  - L11 “Monarchy” · `card.government.011.c3` (text): Why people went along with it / Remember Weber's three roots of authority from Level 3? A monarch who inherits the throne was his example of traditional authority: power accepted because things have always been done this way. Many monarchs had something extra on their side. Britannica notes that successful and popular monarchs were believed to have a sacred right to rule.
  - L93 “Speaking to Your Representative” · `card.government.093.c3` (text): Step two: go and talk / Most MPs also hold surgeries in their constituency: sessions where you can meet them and talk through a problem. Remember Level 3's legal-rational authority, which belongs to the office and not the person? That's why this works. You're not begging a favor from a stranger. You're using an office that exists partly to hear you.
  - L98 “Myths About Government” · `card.government.098.c4` (text): Myth 3: your representative only works for their voters / Level 93 already busted this one. UK MPs are elected to represent everyone who lives in their constituency, whether they voted for them or not. Winning an election puts someone in an office, and Level 3's legal-rational authority belongs to the office, not to its fan club.
- **Tested by:**
  - L3 `question.government.003.q2`: A newly elected official is obeyed because the rules give that office its powers. Which kind of authority is that? → **Legal-rational**
  - L10 `question.government.010.q4`: Back to Level 3: a monarch who inherits the throne holds which kind of authority, in Weber's scheme? → **Traditional**
  - L93 `question.government.093.q3`: Level 3 said legal-rational authority belongs to the office, not the person. How does that help you at an MP's surgery? → **You meet the office, which exists to serve constituents**
  - L100 `question.government.100.q10`: UK civil servants serve any elected government equally well. Which of Weber's kinds of authority does that reflect? → **Legal-rational**
- **Fact-check (2026-09-25):** corroborated. OpenStax gives an inheriting British monarch for traditional, Napoleon and Martin Luther King Jr. among charismatic examples, and says legal-rational authority resides in the office. SEP describes legal-rational authority as impersonal rules independent of personality. ### ☐ `fact.government.election_moe_lead_double`: unverified

> **Claim:** The margin of error on the gap between two candidates is roughly double: a 3-point margin for each becomes about 6 points for a lead, so a 5-point lead could really be anywhere from -1 to +11.

- **Fact-check (2026-09-25):** corroborated. Senate.gov: Rule 22 adopted 1917 allowed cloture by two-thirds; in 1975 reduced to three-fifths of senators duly chosen and sworn, 60 of 100.   - L4 “What a Law Is” · `card.government.004.c2` (text): Rules versus laws / Your household might ban shoes indoors. That's a rule, but not a law. Britannica describes law as the rules of conduct that a community recognizes as binding, enforced through a controlling authority. Two things make the difference: the whole community is bound by it, and an authority (Level 3's accepted power) stands ready to enforce it.
  - L7 “The Social Contract” · `card.government.007.c3` (text): Locke: government works for you / John Locke saw it differently. Even without government, he argued, people have natural rights to life, liberty and property. Government gets its legitimacy from the consent of the governed, and if rulers violate those rights, people may resist them. Remember Level 3's authority, power people accept? Locke made that acceptance the whole foundation.
  - L9 “Nations and States” · `card.government.009.c3` (text): Weber's test for a state / Remember Max Weber from Level 3? In 1919 he defined the state as a human community that successfully claims the monopoly of the legitimate use of physical force within a territory. Only the state gets to use force, through police and courts, and people accept that it's allowed to. It's Level 3's authority, stretched across a whole country.
  - L10 “Checkpoint: Why Government?” · `card.government.010.c3` (comparison): Chapter 1 in three questions: Why rules? (So everyone plays the same game, from football to traffic; Laws bind a whole community and are enforced) vs Who decides? (Authority: power people accept as legitimate; The social contract asks why we obey) vs Who pays, and who does what? (Compulsory taxes fund public services; National, regional and local layers share the work)
  - L10 “Checkpoint: Why Government?” · `card.government.010.c4` (text): Back at the helm / Level 1 began with a ship. Now you can name its parts. The rules of the voyage are laws. Whoever holds the wheel needs authority, and the social contract asks why the crew goes along. The cargo everyone shares is public services. Taxes pay for the fuel. And the crew works on several decks at once, from the national government to the village council.
  - L13 “Dictatorship” · `card.government.013.c3` (text): How dictators hold on / Modern dictators typically take power by force or fraud, Britannica notes, then keep it through intimidation, terror and the suppression of basic civil liberties. They also use mass propaganda to keep public support. Put that in Level 3's terms. Fear gives them power; propaganda is the effort to make it look like authority, power that people accept.
  - L37 “Who Gets to Vote” · `card.government.037.c4` (text): A world standard: universal and equal / Level 34's Declaration set a benchmark in 1948. Article 21 says the will of the people shall be the basis of the authority of government, expressed in periodic and genuine elections by universal and equal suffrage, held by secret vote. Recall Level 3: authority is power people accept as legitimate. Article 21 names elections as the way that acceptance is expressed.
  - L61 “Why Elections?” · `card.government.061.c4` (text): The UN: where authority comes from / In 1948 the Universal Declaration of Human Rights put a third answer in writing. Article 21 says the will of the people shall be the basis of the authority of government, expressed in periodic and genuine elections. Remember Level 3? Authority is power people accept as legitimate. Elections measure that acceptance again and again instead of assuming it. Locke's consent of the governed, on a timetable.
  - L70 “Checkpoint: Elections” · `card.government.070.c3` (text): From a ballot to power / Follow one vote through this chapter. It's cast in secret, turned into seats by a voting system and a district map, fought over in a campaign and counted in the open. What comes out is Level 3's authority: power people accept as legitimate. And Popper's point makes it complete: the ruled can dismiss their rulers without bloodshed, so next time the same vote can take that power away.
  - L77 “Corruption” · `card.government.077.c2` (text): Borrowed power, misused / Transparency International defines corruption as the abuse of entrusted power for private gain. Every word matters. Entrusted: the power was lent to an official by the public. Abuse: it was used for something it wasn't lent for. Private gain: the official pockets the benefit. Remember Level 3? Authority is power people accept. Corruption quietly turns it into a price list.

  - L61 `question.government.061.q3`: Level 3 said authority is power people accept as legitimate. What does UDHR Article 21 make the basis of government's authority? → **The will of the people, shown in elections**
  - L68 `question.government.068.q3`: Level 3 said authority is power people accept as legitimate. How does counting in front of every candidate's agents help the winner? → **Every side can watch, so the result is easier to accept**
  - L77 `question.government.077.q3`: Level 3 said authority is power people accept as legitimate. In those terms, what does a corrupt official do? → **Uses power the public entrusted to them for private gain**

### ☐ `fact.government.un_sc_binding_veto`: unverified

- **Appears in:**
  - L84 “The United Nations” · `card.government.084.c4` (text): Fifteen seats, five vetoes / Keeping the peace is mainly the Security Council's job. It has 15 members, 5 of them permanent: China, France, Russia, the UK and the US. Unlike the Assembly's recommendations, its decisions bind every UN member. > **Claim:** When a treaty needs ratification, signing it does not yet bind a state; ratification is the international act by which a state consents to be bound.

- **Appears in:**
  - L83 “Treaties” · `card.government.083.c3` (text): Sign first, bind later / Signing is often not the last step. When a treaty needs ratification, a signature doesn't bind the state yet; ratification is the act by which a state consents to be bound. In between, a signer must not do anything that would defeat the treaty's purpose, unless it makes clear it won't join. The pen says "we mean to"; ratification says "we will".
  - L84 “The United Nations” · `card.government.084.c2` (text): Signed in San Francisco / Delegates from 50 countries spent two months in San Francisco in 1945 drawing up the UN Charter. The UN came into existence on 24 October 1945, once China, France, the Soviet Union, the UK, the US and most other signers had ratified it. Ratified: Level 83's step, the one that turns a signature into a binding promise.
  - L90 “Checkpoint: Countries and the World” · `card.government.090.c4` (comparison): Chapter 9 in three questions: How do countries talk? (Embassies represent, negotiate and report; Their premises can't be entered without consent) vs How do they make promises? (Treaties bind once a state ratifies; Agreements must be kept in good faith) vs How do they settle disputes? (The ICJ hears states that consent; The ICC tries individuals for the gravest crimes)
- **Tested by:**

## The 1951 Refugee Convention (UNHCR)

- **Source:** `source.unhcr_1951_convention`
- **URL:** https://www.unhcr.org/about-unhcr/overview/1951-refugee-convention
- **License:** reference_only · **Accessed:** 2026-09-25 · **Source record checked (URL/licence):** no

### ☐ `fact.government.refugee_1951_definition`: unverified

> **Claim:** The 1951 Refugee Convention defines a refugee as someone outside their own country who, owing to a well-founded fear of persecution for their race, religion, nationality, membership of a particular social group or political opinion, cannot or will not accept its protection.

- **Concept:** Who is a refugee (`concept.government.refugee_definition`)
- **Appears in:**
  - L88 “Refugees” · `card.government.088.c2` (text): Who counts as a refugee / Today's rule comes from the 1951 Refugee Convention. A refugee is someone outside their own country who can't or won't return to its protection because of a well-founded fear of being persecuted for their race, religion, nationality, membership of a particular social group or political opinion. And UNHCR says refugee status is declaratory: you're a refugee from the moment you meet the criteria, before any official says so.
  - L88 “Refugees” · `card.government.088.c4` (fact): Most people forced from home never cross a border. / UNHCR's Global Trends report counted 117.8 million people forcibly displaced at the end of 2025. Of them, 41.6 million were refugees and 68.7 million were displaced inside their own countries. Because the 1951 definition requires being outside your own country, those 68.7 million aren't refugees in law, even though they fled home too.
- **Tested by:**
  - L88 `question.government.088.q3`: UNHCR says refugee status is declaratory. Which Level 81 rule about states works the same way? → **A state's existence doesn't depend on recognition**
  - L90 `question.government.090.q5`: Back to Level 88: who of these is a refugee under the 1951 Convention? → **Someone who fled persecution to another country**
- **Fact-check (2026-09-25):** corroborated. Article 1A(2) of the convention text (University of Minnesota Human Rights Library); UNHCR's convention page and emergency handbook quote the same definition. Sources: https://hrlibrary.umn.edu/instree/v1crs.htm, https://www.unhcr.org/about-unhcr/overview/1951-refugee-convention, https://emergency.unhcr.org/protection/legal-framework/refugee-definition

## How to Engage in Budget Cycles and Processes to Leverage Government Budgets for Children (PF4C Technical Guidance Note No. 1) (UNICEF)

- **Source:** `source.unicef_budget_cycles_2016`
- **URL:** https://www.unicef.org/sites/default/files/2019-12/Engaging_in_Budget_Cycles_and_Processes_FINAL.pdf
- **License:** reference_only · **Accessed:** 2026-09-25 · **Source record checked (URL/licence):** no

### ☐ `fact.government.budget_cycle_four_stages`: unverified

> **Claim:** The budget cycle usually has four stages: the executive prepares the plan; the legislature debates, amends and approves it; the government carries it out; and the actual spending is audited and assessed.

- **Concept:** The four-stage budget cycle (`concept.government.budget_cycle_stages`)
- **Appears in:**
  - L71 “Government Budgets” · `card.government.071.c3` (timeline): Four stages, every year: 1. Prepare: The executive, the government of the day, puts the plan together; 2. Approve: The legislature debates it, amends it and votes on it; 3. Carry out: The government collects the money and spends it; 4. Audit: Auditors check what was actually spent, and whether it worked
  - L79 “The Military” · `card.government.079.c3` (text): Civilians in charge / In a democracy, the armed forces answer to democratically elected authorities, overseen by the courts, the media and civil society. Civilians decide the military's missions, size, budget and purchases; commanders decide how to carry the missions out. Parliaments add laws, hearings and control of the purse, so Level 71's approval stage applies to tanks too.
  - L80 “Checkpoint: Money and Government” · `card.government.080.c1` (text): Every budget ends the same way: someone checks the receipts. / Level 71's cycle had a fourth stage, audit, where the actual spending is checked. This chapter followed the money from taxes to pensions, bridges and tanks. This level follows the people who follow the money.
  - L80 “Checkpoint: Money and Government” · `card.government.080.c3` (text): Follow one euro / Try it with a single euro of tax. It arrives on the collecting side of Level 71's budget. The biggest share of spending goes on social protection, so it may well end up in someone's pension. If the government spent more than it collected, some of what it spent was borrowed. And after the year ends, an auditor checks that the money went where the budget said.
  - L80 “Checkpoint: Money and Government” · `card.government.080.c4` (comparison): Chapter 8 on one receipt: Raise and borrow (Compulsory taxes pay for most of it; Deficits are borrowed, and pile up as debt) vs Plan and spend (Prepare, approve, carry out, audit; Social protection is the biggest slice) vs Check (Independent auditors check spending; Bodies like Hong Kong's ICAC fight corruption)
- **Tested by:**
  - L80 `question.government.080.q3`: Money and Government recap: in Level 71's four-stage budget cycle, what comes right after the legislature approves the plan? → **The government carries it out**
- **Fact-check (2026-09-25):** corroborated. ParlAmericas' 'National Budget Cycle' handout and a 2025 European Parliament study describe the same stages: executive preparation, legislative approval, execution, then audit and assessment. Sources: http://www.parlamericas.org/uploads/documents/Handout-2-Budget-Cycle_ENG.pdf, https://www.europarl.europa.eu/RegData/etudes/STUD/2025/779113/BUDG_STU(2025)779113_EN.pdf

### ☐ `fact.government.budget_plan_two_sides`: unverified

> **Claim:** A government budget is a plan setting out the revenue a government expects to collect and the spending it intends for the coming year.

- **Appears in:**
  - L71 “Government Budgets” · `card.government.071.c2` (text): A plan in a bag / The word comes from Old French bougette, a small leather bag: picture a finance minister opening his wallet to reveal his plans. Britain's chancellor still holds up a red box on Budget Day. Inside is a plan with two sides: the money the government expects to collect, much of it Level 6's compulsory taxes, and the money it intends to spend over the coming year.
  - L78 “Deficits and Debt” · `card.government.078.c2` (text): The yearly gap / Level 71's budget has two sides. When spending beats revenue, the gap is a deficit; the reverse is a surplus. To cover a deficit, a government borrows, mostly by selling bonds: 79.3% of OECD public debt takes that form. Run deficits year after year and they pile up as debt.
  - L80 “Checkpoint: Money and Government” · `card.government.080.c3` (text): Follow one euro / Try it with a single euro of tax. It arrives on the collecting side of Level 71's budget. The biggest share of spending goes on social protection, so it may well end up in someone's pension. If the government spent more than it collected, some of what it spent was borrowed. And after the year ends, an auditor checks that the money went where the budget said.
